sentences.text: Alioramus is characterized by five bony crests on its snout, a high tooth count, and a low skull.
The skull of Alioramus remotus was approximately 45 centimeters long.
According to Kurzanov's original work, Alioramus was a medium-sized carnivore reaching up to six meters in length and 2.4 meters in height.
In 2016, Molina-Pérez and Larramendi estimated Alioramus remotus at 5.5 meters and 500 kg, and Alioramus altai at 5 meters and 385 kg.

The team noted that in terms of body size, the holotype was closer to a seven/eight-year-old Albertosaurus or Gorgosaurus, and a five/six-year-old Daspletosaurus or Tyrannosaurus, suggesting Alioramus attained a comparably smaller adult size.
Alioramus was first described by Kurzanov in 1976.
The type species Alioramus remotus was named and described by Sergei Kurzanov in 1976.
The holotype of Alioramus was found in the Nemegt Formation at Nogon-Tsav by a Soviet-Mongolian expedition in the early 1970s.
The fossil material for Alioramus altai was discovered in 2001 at the Tsagan Khushu locality in the Nemegt Formation.
Alioramus were bipedal carnivores with sharp teeth.
Alioramus possessed a locking mechanism in its lower jaw similar to Tarbosaurus, reducing flexibility compared to other tyrannosaurids.
Brusatte and colleagues in 2009 indicated that Alioramus lacks robust skull traits like a deep maxilla or peg-like teeth necessary for the "puncture-pull" feeding style of large tyrannosaurids.
Nemegt sediments preserve floodplains and large river channels, but caliche deposits indicate periodic droughts.
The Nogon Tsav fauna was similar to Nemegt's, potentially including troodontids, pachycephalosaurs, ankylosaurs, and hadrosaurs, alongside saltasaurs which were prey for Nemegt theropods.
A 2003 analysis classified Alioramus within the family Tyrannosauridae and subfamily Tyrannosaurinae.
The description of Qianzhousaurus in 2014 established the tribe Alioramini, which includes Alioramus.
The genus authority for Alioramus is Kurzanov, 1976.
Another study omitted Alioramus entirely due to the fragmentary nature of its remains.
Alioramus lived during the Late Cretaceous period in Asia.
Although never radiometrically dated, the fauna suggests Alioramus lived during the Maastrichtian of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 70 to 65 million years ago.
A 2004 study suggested Alioramus might belong outside the family Tyrannosauridae, reflecting a more basal position within Tyrannosauroidea.
A second analysis found Alioramini to be the sister group of Tyrannosauridae, outside the clade including Albertosaurinae and Tyrannosaurinae.
It remains a mystery why Alioramins remained confined to Asia and did not colonize North America until more evidence is discovered.
It is debated whether the known specimen is a juvenile or an adult with a deformed skull, which affects estimates of total body length, as no confirmed adult specimens are known.
The long, low skull shape suggests Alioramus may not have reached maturity when it died and could even be a juvenile Tarbosaurus, as they lived in the same time and place.
